paras: The notice runs to about a hundred and forty words and nobody appears in it. A fault has been identified. One batch was traced to a single production line. Eleven thousand units are affected, customers are asked to check a reference number, and affected units will be replaced at no cost. Seven verbs, no people. Read it out loud and you notice something strange: it describes a great deal of work and not one person who did any of it.

That is not laziness, and it is not, in this case, cowardice. Rachel Osei has written more than sixty of these documents in eleven years, and her argument is simple. “The notice is about the product. The moment you put a name in it, the reader stops checking whether they own one of these and starts looking for somebody to be angry with. That is a worse outcome for everyone, including the person you named.” The internal record, she points out, is the exact opposite: names, dates, and who signed off on what, line by line. Two documents, two jobs.

Then there is the other use, and everybody recognises it. Mistakes were made. The decision was taken. It was felt that further action was not required. The grammar is identical to the notice, and the effect is not. A researcher at a business school ran the comparison directly: two versions of the same incident report, one saying that a named manager approved the batch, the other saying the batch was approved, everything else word for word the same. Readers of the second version estimated a lower cost, and were markedly less likely to say that anybody should lose their job.

What makes the finding uncomfortable is that it does not require anybody to be dishonest. The effect is the same whether the writer chose the form to hide a person or simply wrote the way reports are always written. The wording does its work either way, which is precisely why it is worth knowing. Somebody who flagged a problem in February and watched nothing happen until June has a legitimate interest in whether the eventual report says it was flagged or says who flagged it, and to whom.

Osei is not defensive about any of this. She keeps a rule she describes as unglamorous and effective: every passive sentence in a draft has to survive one question, which is whether she could name the agent if somebody asked her tomorrow. If she can, and leaving the name out is a matter of focus, the sentence stays. If she cannot — if the passive exists because nobody wants to find out — the sentence goes back. “It is not about grammar,” she says. “It is about whether the sentence is deliberate or just convenient.”

listenings.text: People love to attack this kind of writing. They call it cowardly. They say it exists so that nobody has to take responsibility, and I understand why it sounds that way, but I want to defend it for one specific document. A public safety notice is about the product. It is not about me and it is not about the person who approved the batch in November. The moment you put a name in that notice, the reader stops doing the only thing the notice exists for, which is checking whether they own one of the affected units, and starts looking for somebody to be angry with. That is a worse outcome for everybody, including the person you just named. Now, the internal report is a completely different animal, and I want to be clear about this. That one has names in it. It has dates. It has who signed off on what, line by line, and it is the document that gets read if anybody is ever held accountable. Two documents. Two jobs. The mistake people make is judging one of them by the standards of the other.

A researcher at a business school ran a study that is very simple and slightly uncomfortable. Two groups of participants read an incident report about a product failure. The reports were word for word identical except in one sentence. In the first version, a named manager approved the batch. In the second version, the batch was approved. That is the entire difference. One name, present or absent. The group who read the version with no name estimated a substantially lower financial cost for the incident, and they were markedly less likely to say that anybody should lose their job over it. Now here is the part I find genuinely interesting. The finding does not tell you anything about the writer's intentions. It does not prove that anybody was hiding anything. The effect is exactly the same whether the form was chosen deliberately to protect somebody, or whether the writer simply wrote the way reports have always been written in that company. The sentence does the work either way, and the reader has no way of knowing which one it was. That is the reason to know about it, whichever end of the document you are standing at.
